implementation_notes: Python needs no locator class: a module-level dict plus a register decorator (or a class attribute map) is the registry, and because importing a module executes it once, the dict is already a process-wide singleton - the module namespace replaces the ServiceLocator object. The same shape scales from a handful of hard-wired implementations to a factory map keyed by a configuration string, and a small resolve() function at the boundary turns an unknown key into a clear exception instead of an AttributeError three frames later. For application code, prefer passing the callable or object in from main; keep the dict form for the seams that cannot be injected.
pitfalls: The dict is module-global: tests that register different doubles interfere with each other unless they clean up, so give tests an isolated registry object rather than mutating the shared one.
Decorator registration runs at import time, so the registry's contents depend on which modules were imported - a missing import looks like an unknown service at run time.
Keying by bare strings loses the compile-time link; keep keys as module-level constants so typos are greppable and rename-safe.

variants.name: Entry-point discovery via importlib.metadata
variants.implementation_notes: When third-party packages must contribute implementations without edits to the host, the registry is installed-package metadata: distributions declare [project.entry-points."acme.renderers"] in pyproject.toml and the host resolves entry_points(group="acme.renderers") and calls EntryPoint.load() to import the declared object. That is the discovery mechanism behind console scripts, pip plugins and pytest's pluggy ecosystem; it replaces both the hand-written registry and the import-time registration step with packaging metadata. Cache the resolved set, keep the group name in one constant, and treat a failing load() as a plugin error rather than as a missing service.
pitfalls: entry_points() reflects what the environment reports as installed: removing or upgrading a distribution without reinstalling can leave a group entry whose load() raises ImportError.
Loading every entry point eagerly imports arbitrary third-party code during startup; load per name when startup cost or trust boundaries matter.
A wrong group name silently yields an empty set - an empty registry must be an error at startup, not an empty feature at run time.
